title: Smile and Cellar
premise: Folklorist Edmund Voss arrives in the isolated village of Hollowmere to record its dying songs, only to hear a bell toll from a church that has stood empty since its bell was melted for scrap in 1911. The villagers hum a harvest song with a final verse no one will sing aloud, and Edmund realizes each singer who once performed it in full vanished, remembered by no one but the bell. As he digs into parish records and the memories of the village's oldest woman, he learns the bell was cast with the names of six drowned children and rings each autumn to claim a seventh voice to complete its chorus. In the climax, Edmund refuses to sing the last verse alone and instead teaches it to the whole village, so the debt is shared and the bell, unable to choose one throat, falls silent forever—leaving Hollowmere bound together by a grief they finally speak aloud.
about_author: Dominic Fairweather is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing parish records in rural England before turning to fiction. His novels blend meticulous historical detail with folk horror, exploring what communities bury to survive.

chapters.title: The Road That Forgets Itself
chapters.summary: Edmund Voss arrives in Hollowmere on foot, his recorder and notebooks in hand, determined to document songs before the village's last elders die. The bus driver refuses to go past the crossroads after dark. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: detached professional curiosity masking a loneliness he won't name.

chapters.title: A Village of Closed Mouths
chapters.summary: Edmund canvasses the village and meets polite refusals; every household claims to know no songs. Only the publican, Marta Hale, offers lodging—and one warning: never ask about the church. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: frustration hardening into stubborn resolve.

chapters.title: What the Bell Did Not Do
chapters.summary: In the parish archive, Edmund finds the 1911 record: the bell sold and melted down. Yet at dusk, a single toll rolls across the valley from the roofless tower. No one else looks up. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: the first crack in his rationalism.

chapters.title: The Song They Hum Half Of
chapters.summary: Marta's grandmother, old Ivy Thorne, hums a harvest melody but stops before the final verse, hands trembling. She says her mother sang it whole in 1938 and was gone by morning, unremembered except by Ivy. POV: Edmund interviewing Ivy. Emotional beat: dread arriving through tenderness.

chapters.title: Six Names in Bronze
chapters.summary: Edmund uncovers the bell's founding inscription: six children drowned in the millpond in 1909, their names cast into the metal. The foundry ledger lists a seventh name, scratched out. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: scholarly excitement curdling into horror.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Missed
chapters.summary: Edmund finds a 1954 newspaper clipping about a missing surveyor whose landlady insisted no such man had ever lodged there. The description matches a photograph in the church vestry. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: cold recognition—he is following a pattern.

chapters.title: Marta's Silence
chapters.summary: Edmund confronts Marta; she admits the village knows what the bell does and chooses forgetting as survival. Her own father rang the warning each year until he stopped speaking entirely. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: guilt and complicity exposed.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Ivy agrees to teach Edmund the first five verses on condition he mouth the sixth silently. He transcribes it: an invitation, sung by the bell, answered by a name. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: intimacy with something predatory.

chapters.title: The Tower at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Edmund explores the roofless church and finds the empty bell frame, warm to the touch, and chalk marks counting down years—this year's mark freshly drawn. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: violation, as if the church knows him.

chapters.title: Villagers Who Look Through Him
chapters.summary: Overnight, shopkeepers begin mishearing Edmund's name; a child asks her mother why the stranger's chair is empty. The forgetting has started early this time. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: terror of erasure while still alive.

chapters.title: Ivy's Confession
chapters.summary: Ivy reveals she was meant to be the seventh child in 1911 but the foundryman substituted his own son's name, dooming the bell to hunt forever. She has carried the debt seventy years. POV: Ivy. Emotional beat: exhausted release of a lifelong secret.

chapters.title: The Foundryman's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the foundry's surviving papers, Edmund reads the son's letter refusing to be cast into bronze—and the father's note that a bell must always hold seven voices or take them. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: understanding the mechanism, not yet the escape.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Tolling
chapters.summary: Autumn deepens; the bell rings nightly now, closer, and Edmund wakes with the sixth verse on his lips, nearly sung. Marta nails his window shut against himself. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: the enemy moving inside his own body.

chapters.title: The Choir That Refused
chapters.summary: Edmund proposes the unthinkable: if the whole village sings the verse together, the bell cannot single out one voice. The village council refuses—shared grief, they say, is worse than shared silence. POV: Marta arguing the case. Emotional beat: hope meeting entrenched fear.

chapters.title: What Happened to the Surveyor's Recorder
chapters.summary: Edmund recovers the 1954 surveyor's hidden tape from the church wall: on it, the man sings the sixth verse alone, and the recording captures a second voice answering. POV: Edmund listening. Emotional beat: grief for the dead stranger, and proof the trap is real.

chapters.title: Ivy Decides
chapters.summary: Ivy announces she will sing the verse herself and end it, sparing Edmund. Edmund refuses to let another name be spent in his place—the theme crystallizes: justice outside law means refusing lawful sacrifice. POV: Ivy then Edmund. Emotional beat: fierce, mutual defiance.

chapters.title: Breaking the Council
chapters.summary: Edmund plays the 1954 tape at the village meeting; hearing the answering voice, half the village remembers people they'd lost to the bell and weeps. The council's wall of forgetting cracks. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: collective mourning as rebellion.

chapters.title: The Night Before Harvest
chapters.summary: On the eve of the bell's claiming night, the village rehearses the sixth verse in whispers, imperfect and off-key. Ivy teaches the children first. POV: multiple villagers briefly, anchored by Edmund. Emotional beat: fragile found-family solidarity.

chapters.title: The Tolling Hour
chapters.summary: At midnight the bell rings full peal for the first time since 1911, and the empty tower fills with six small voices calling for a seventh. Edmund stands in the churchyard, throat burning with the unsung verse. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: peak terror and resolve.

chapters.title: One Hundred Voices
chapters.summary: As the bell demands his name, the entire village steps into the churchyard and sings the sixth verse together—a hundred throats where the bell needs one. The choice paralyzes it; the bronze cracks along the founders' inscription. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: triumphant, terrifying unity.

chapters.title: Silence, and What Remains
chapters.summary: Dawn shows the tower empty and cold; the six children's names are read aloud for the first time, and Ivy finally weeps for the foundryman's son. The village keeps singing the song—now all six verses, together, every harvest. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: grief transformed into ritual and belonging.

chapters.title: The Folklorist Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Edmund publishes nothing, instead staying in Hollowmere as its keeper of songs, teaching newcomers the rule: never sing it alone. On the last page, far away, another village's melted bell gives a single, patient toll. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: peace shadowed by vigilance—memory as ongoing duty.
